In the second fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, King Prasenajit’s ugly daughter, named Vajrā— translated into Chinese as "Vajra" (Diamond)— asks:
"If you take the diamond as a metaphor for prajñā, what is the significance of this?"
The answer is:
Just as among worldly treasures, the diamond is foremost;
so too, among supramundane treasures, Prajñā is foremost.
Furthermore, just as no person in the world can appraise the value of a diamond gem,
so too no person in the world can measure the merit produced by the Jewel of the Dharma of Prajñā.

Furthermore, it is like a vajra jewel: whether placed upon a mountain peak or on level ground, it passes straight through without obstruction until it reaches the vajra-limit, where, being of the same nature, it comes to rest.

The Prajñā-vajra is likewise: when placed upon the summit of the mountain of merit, it passes directly across the plain of sin without obstruction, reaching the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—neither sin nor merit, neither existent nor non-existent—abiding therein as being of the same nature.
Furthermore, just as a worldly diamond jewel is transparent and pure, Master Kumārajīva said:
"A diamond within the square inch [of the heart] illuminates for dozens of li, such that all things are reflected therein."
Prajñā is also like this: it illuminates the water of the true mark (lakṣaṇa), making it clear and pure.
Furthermore, just as no sentient being—except for Nārāyaṇa—is able to grasp a vajra jewel;

so too is prajñā: except for those who possess the great power of insight through faith, awakening, non-reliance, and non-attainment, those who delight in inferior dharmas or sentient beings attached to views cannot believe in or uphold it.

As the sutra says: "It is taught for those who have set out in the Mahāyāna, and for those who have set out in the Supreme Vehicle. Those who delight in inferior teachings and are attached to various views will be unable to believe and uphold it.
Furthermore, it is like a man who swallows a small diamond; it remains undigested throughout his entire life.
Prajñā is likewise: if one can fully realize that which is indestructible, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who obtain the vajra-jewel, they will be far removed from all poverty and suffering, and enjoy every form of peace and happiness;
likewise, if they obtain Prajñā, they will leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, just as wherever a vajra jewel is located, it can neutralize evil spirits and all kinds of sorcery;
so too is Prajñā: wherever it is present, the Māras, non-Buddhists, and evil spirits cannot find an opportunity to harm.
Furthermore, just as a diamond jewel completely shatters all other objects while the diamond itself suffers no fracture or loss, so too is prajñā:
it is able to completely shatter all afflictions without itself suffering any loss.
Furthermore, Vajra, no material object whatsoever can destroy it;
likewise, Prajñā cannot be destroyed by any disputants or by any afflictions.
Furthermore, just as a diamond jewel does not have a fixed color when placed in the sunlight, so too is Prajñāpāramitā indeterminate within the great assembly;

it is sometimes called a cause and sometimes called a fruit. To those of small minds it is called "small," while to those of great minds it is called "great. In relation to objects it is called "objects," and in relation to wisdom it is called "wisdom. Since this Prajñā has no fixed characteristic, the verse says: "Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha speaks of it by various names; According to the capacities of sentient beings, he establishes different designations for it."
Furthermore, just as a vajra jewel possesses such various superior functions yet never has the thought, "I am superior," so too is prajñā:
although it possesses immeasurable and manifold merits, it never has such a thought; therefore, prajñā is inconceivable.
Question:
From where does the vajra emerge? Answer:
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "Just as gold is extracted from ore, and the diamond is extracted from gold," thus we know that the essence within gold is called the diamond (*vajra*).
Question:
What are the similarities and differences between a vajra and a celestial cintāmaṇi? Answer:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When Śakra held a vajra in his hand to battle the asuras, it shattered and fell to Jambudvīpa, where it was transformed into a cintāmaṇi. The *Vibhāṣā* states: "A vajra can shatter crystal mountains and even cintāmaṇis. Thus, we know they are distinct.
Furthermore, this clarifies that while Prajñā is identical to the vajra, this Prajñā transcends the vajra and cannot be compared to it.
The vajra is a worldly object; Prajñā is not worldly.
If one loses it, one grieves; if one gains it, one rejoices.
One who has attained Prajñā has neither grief nor joy.
A diamond is an insentient object; [Prajñā is not like this].
Prajñā is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know; its immeasurable merits have now been briefly explained.
Furthermore, some say that within the Śrāvaka-dharma, from the emptiness of conventional designations up to the stage of Arhat, it is collectively termed "vajra."
Within the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, from the final stage of the thirty minds up to the wisdom of a Buddha, it is collectively termed "vajra.
If discussed specifically, however, from the first bhūmi onward until the wisdom of a Buddha, it is only then called "true vajra."

Why is this so? Because those at the stage of the thirty minds are merely practicing with delusion and have not yet attained true non-delusion; they merely suppress afflictions and have not yet severed them. Since characteristics still follow into the essence, they have not yet attained what is called the "True Vajra"; nevertheless, they may be designated as "Vajra" by virtue of these characteristics.

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one attains the understanding of the true and the false; this is precisely what enables the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the phenomenal marks do not enter into the essence, this is the "True Vajra.

As for the traditional practice of using the mind that has reached the ultimate limit of study as a metaphor for the *vajra*, this is based on the doctrine of Kaishan: once the subduing of afflictions is complete, there remains the fundamental grade of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the most difficult to subdue. Only the mind that has reached the ultimate limit of study can subdue it; therefore, upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, the Buddha-wisdom arises to sever it.
For this reason, the mind that exhausts its study is called "vajra.
Furthermore, some say:
because the mind that exhausts its study is precisely able to sever delusions, it is named "vajra."
Such statements all assert that there are delusions to be severed and a wisdom capable of severing them; for this reason, they are termed "having attainment.
Because they involve attainment, one cannot sever delusions, and thus there is no vajra.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Those who perceive something attainable do not proceed from one stage to another.

Furthermore, you say that when afflictions have not yet been severed, there are afflictions but no liberation; whereas at the time when afflictions are severed, there is liberation but no afflictions.
This implies that delusion originally existed but now does not, while awakening originally did not exist but now does; this is the contemplation of arising and ceasing.
As it is said in the sutras: "All dharmas originally existed but now do not," and further: "If dharmas existed previously but do not exist later, then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be at fault."

What is clarified here is that one knows that delusion was originally non-existent and is not non-existent now; one understands that it was originally not non-existent and is not existent now. Therefore, all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, neither bound nor liberated, without observation and without objects; this is what is called *prajñā*.
Question: If this is so, why does the Sūtra say, “The wisdom associated with a single thought-moment severs the afflictions along with their habitual tendencies”? Answer:
If one perceives arising and ceasing, then one cannot sever [the afflictions];
because one thoroughly understands that all phenomena are neither understood nor deluded, and are neither severed nor not severed, the afflictions are thereby severed.
Question:
Does the diamond serve as a metaphor only for *prajñā*, or does it also serve as a metaphor for other dharmas? Answer:

The *Vajracchedikā* employs various analogies; in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Dharma-body is likened to a "vajra-body," and samādhi is likened to "vajra-samādhi"—these analogies take meditative concentration as the vajra.
Here, however, wisdom is likened to the vajra.
Question:
Is vajra a treasure of the heavens, or is it a treasure of humans? Answer:
Humanity and the heavens possess this, just as the golden wheel of a Cakravartin King; because it is a vajra-jewel, everything it strikes is shattered.
When Śakra wields the vajra to battle the Asuras, it is likewise a treasure of the heavens.
Third, the explanation of *prajñā*.
*Prajñā* is a foreign term; there are two textual traditions in the *Śāstra*:
first, "Prajñā, in the language of Qin, means wisdom (*jñāna*)," which opens up the skillful application of it.
The subsequent text states: "Prajñā is profound and heavy, while wisdom (hui-zhi) is light and thin; one cannot weigh profound and heavy Prajñā with light and thin wisdom.
Master Zhuangyan said:
"The name 'Prajñā' encompasses five meanings, whereas 'wisdom' is but a single strand; it is not a correct translation."
Regarding the interpretation of "wisdom" (*jñāna*), the sūtras and śāstras differ.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* explains it by dividing it into two characters:
knowing the mental inclinations of sentient beings and preaching the Dharma accordingly constitutes the activity of wisdom (*jñāna-karman*).
Neither grasping nor rejecting, one enters the gate of the single characteristic and gives rise to the karma of wisdom (*prajñā-karman*).
An ancient commentary on this passage states:

"Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the understanding of existence, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is the understanding of emptiness; furthermore, knowledge is for the sake of transforming others, while wisdom is for one's own cultivation."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"the wisdom of the path (*mārga-jñatā*), the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārga-ākāra-jñatā*), all-knowledge (*sarva-jñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākāra-jñatā*).
These names for wisdom thus encompass both emptiness and existence.

Furthermore, the cause is termed "wisdom" (prajñā) and the fruit is designated as "knowledge" (jñāna); for example, the cause is termed "path-wisdom" (mārga-prajñā) and "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (mārgākāra-jñāna), while the fruit is designated as "all-knowledge" (sarvajña) and "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā).

Furthermore, "wisdom" (jñāna) is said to encompass both cause and result, as in the meaning of the three types of wisdom: the *sarvajñatā* of the śrāvaka, the *mārgajñatā* of the bodhisattva, and the *sarvākārajñatā* of the Buddha.
Furthermore, "wisdom" (prajñā) is said to encompass both cause and effect; as the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The great wisdom that is equal in all Buddhas.

The text of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains the two characters "wisdom" (hui) and "knowledge" (zhi) together, stating that true wisdom is called "knowledge," and further explaining that "wisdom" refers to a person of knowledge.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "wisdom" (hui): the sūtras state that the knowledge of liberation is the meaning of wisdom; therefore, "knowledge" (zhi) is synonymous with "wisdom.
Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* contains two passages:
"Prajñā, in the language of Qin, means wisdom (hui)," and elsewhere it says, "In the language of Qin, it means wisdom-knowledge (zhihui)."
Question:

Why do the scriptures and treatises sometimes emerge and sometimes submerge, at times converging and at times diverging, rather than clearly indicating a single path to people? Would it not be better to provide a clear exposition so that understanding may be attained?

Answer: It is not that the Sages are unable to clearly demonstrate the path to people through a single approach; however, that there are now words spoken of "appearing and disappearing" carries a profound meaning.

This is because sentient beings inherently possess a mind of grasping and attachment; by reason of these causes and conditions, they are bound to Māra, their birth and death are unceasing, and the wheel of existence constantly turns. Thus, they do not awaken to the Middle Way, the Buddha-nature, or the right contemplation of Prajñā.

If one were now to provide a definitive exposition of a single path as the ultimate truth, it would only further increase the mind’s attachment; therefore, the teachings appear and disappear indeterminately to stir the root-consciousness of birth and death, causing one to awaken suddenly to the True Dharma. Thus, the indeterminate teaching is of profound benefit.
If a student rigidly adheres to a single passage from a scripture or treatise to establish their own sectarian doctrine, they are merely a follower of Māra.
Furthermore, sentient beings do not belong to a single land, possess a single faculty-nature, or have a single spiritual friend; for this reason, the Buddhas teach the Dharma in various ways.
Question:
The name "prajñā" is already known; what is the essence of prajñā? Answer:
The proponents of the *Dilun* school assert that there are two kinds of *prajñā*:
first, the *prajñā* of true cultivation, which is the eighth consciousness;
second, the *prajñā* of conditional cultivation, which is the seventh consciousness.
The masters of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* say:
"The mind that takes the ultimate truth as its object forgets its own state and severs all signs.
This mind of liberation is the essence of *prajñā*."
The Abhidharma masters say:
"The essence of *prajñā* is the characteristic of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that takes the principles of the Four Noble Truths as its object.
These three interpretations are currently widespread; they must all be thoroughly refuted and clarified, as is explained in detail in the *Great Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra Commentary* (*Dapin xuán*).

However, as this sutra is widely recited in the world today, I shall now briefly state its essential phrases, hoping that gentlemen who investigate the profound will grasp what lies beyond the literal meaning.
Question:
What is taken to be *prajñā* (wisdom) now?
Answer: If a practitioner realizes the nature of inversion and attains sudden, clear awakening, this is conventionally designated as *prajñā*.
Question:
This sudden and clear awakening—could this not be the mind?
Answer: This realization is neither the mind nor separate from the mind.
Question:
What is meant by "neither mind nor apart from mind"? Answer:
Since it is said that the mind attains awakening and understanding, how could this be separate from the mind?
Yet, this awakened mind ultimately neither gives rise to the state of having a mind nor the state of having no mind; how then could it be identical to the mind?
Question:
If one says that the mind awakens, this is still the very mind;
if one says that one awakens to this mind and does not grasp at the existence or non-existence of the mind, this is to be free from the mind. Answer:
To still speak of "identity" and "separation" is yet another failure to awaken.
If one were truly awakened, what identity or separation would there ultimately be?
Question:
Since it is neither identical nor distinct, there should be neither delusion nor awakening. Answer:
Because of delusion, one speaks of identity and distinction; because of awakening, one realizes that there is neither identity nor distinction.
Since they are neither identical nor distinct, what, in the end, could there be of delusion or enlightenment?
One may grasp their underlying meaning, but one must not cling to the literal words.
Fourth, the explanation of the *pāramitās*.
*Pāramitā* is translated here as "reaching the other shore.
According to the customs and laws of foreign lands, when any undertaking is brought to completion, it is termed *pāramitā*.
Now, although one who has awakened to the Way may accumulate merit over many kalpas, if they do not obtain *prajñā*, their practice remains unfulfilled.
If one awakens to Prajñā, the myriad practices are fully perfected; therefore, it is named "Pāramitā" (Arrival at the Other Shore). Prajñā asked:
"Since there is already an 'other shore,' why speak of this shore and the midstream?"
Answer:

The Noble Ones merely employ the provisional designation "the other shore" to enable others to awaken and enter through it; why must one necessarily posit this shore, the other shore, and the middle current?

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Though there is no this shore, there is the other shore. This refers precisely to that matter. As for the necessity of an agent, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The view of existence and non-existence is this shore; the wisdom that destroys the views of existence and non-existence is the other shore; and generosity (*dāna*) is the middle current."
Fifth, the explanation of the sūtras.
There are three kinds of sūtras: those where the words constitute the sūtra, those where the principle constitutes the sūtra, and those where both words and principle together constitute the sūtra.
The masters of the *Dilun* school say:
Prior to the thirty stages of mind, human-authored texts serve as the sūtra;
at the thirty stages of mind, the integration of principle and text serves as the sūtra;
from the first stage onward, the application of principle serves as the sūtra.
Now, because it clarifies the principles and causes and conditions through its phrasing, it is called a "sūtra" (jīng), for one realizes the Way by means of the text.
Since it is able to manifest [the truth], the text constitutes the sūtra.
Seventh, the analysis of transmission and translation.
Question:
The colophon at the end of the *Mahākaruṇā-bhikṣuṇī-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* states:
"The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* originally consisted of eight fascicles; now there remains only the single chapter titled 'Comparing Merits' (*Géliàng Gōngdé*)."
What is the meaning of this?
Answer: Such an interpretation is not tenable.
Why is this so? This single fascicle of the sutra was translated by three individuals:
first, Dharma Master Kumārajīva, who translated one fascicle at the Xiaoyao Garden in the fourth year of the Hongshi era.
If there were eight fascicles, why were they not translated?

Second, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha retranslated this work in this land; the sūtra and its commentary together comprise three fascicles. The sūtra includes an additional chapter on faith, while the commentary exhaustively explains the matters and meanings from beginning to end: it first clarifies the meaning of the sūtra’s prologue and the homage, and finally expresses the merit of sympathetic joy and praise.
If there were eight fascicles, for what reason would it stop at explaining only one chapter?
Thirdly, when the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha retranslated this sūtra in Lingnan, the text was concise while the meaning was expansive; he did not state that it consisted of eight fascicles.
Furthermore, since this sutra is complete with the three divisions of introduction, main body, and dissemination, how can it be said to consist of only one chapter?
Question:
The colophon at the end of the *Mahākaruṇā Bhikṣuṇī Pūrvapraṇidhāna Sūtra* also states:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* was first taught, and from within it the *Svalpaprājñāpāramitā* emerged;
later the *Prasphullapraśaṃsā* was taught, and from within it the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* emerged. How is this so?
Answer: This is also not the case.
The "Practice of the Path" (Mārga-caryā) is merely another name for the "Minor Section" (Kṣudraka).

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Prabhāsa-praśaṃsā*, the *Pao-kuang* (Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā), and the *Tao-hsing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā) are listed first, and later they are again listed as the *Piao-p'in* (Svalpākṣara), the *Pao-kuang*, and the *Kuang-ts'an*. Therefore, it is known that *Piao-p'in* is simply another name for the *Tao-hsing*.
Master Rui’s *Preface to the Short Version* states: "This sutra consists of thirty chapters, which are unified by the Way; therefore, it is titled 'Practice of the Way' (*Dàoxíng*).
One should know that the 'Practice of the Way' originated from this Short Version."
Eighth, the clarification of the manifest verification.
Question:
What are the signs and benefits of reciting and upholding the Prajñā?
Answer: This sutra has circulated in the land of Han for over two hundred years; those who have recited it and thereby attained benefit are beyond counting.
Formerly, while a mountain monk was reciting it, he heard a snap of fingers in the air, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
Furthermore, Dharma Master Kaishan was able to recite [the scriptures] for an additional seven years of life.
Also, when Zhu Shiheng was traveling, he cast the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* into a fire; the fire was extinguished by this act, and the scripture remained unburnt.
The vast benefits are immeasurable and cannot be fully recounted.
Ninth, the explanation of the structural divisions (*chapters and sections*).

Regarding this scripture, its phrasing is concise and its principles are profound; those who attempt to explain it rarely grasp its true meaning. Consequently, the structural divisions have become obscured by a cloud of dust and filth, ultimately causing the sun and moon of Prajñā to be eclipsed and lose their brilliance.
I shall now briefly enumerate the various masters to demonstrate their strengths and weaknesses.

To trace the origin: the Great Sage, responding to conditions, expounded the teachings with the intent that they serve as pointers to lead one toward awakening to reality; thus, the ultimate meaning does not reside in the words themselves. Those who aspire to grasp the intended meaning should comprehend its essential conclusion and the locus upon which it relies.
According to the tradition inherited from the Northern Lands, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci provided a twelve-part commentary on the sutra:
first, the Introduction;
second, the Part on Protection and Entrustment.
Third, the stage of abiding;
fourth, the stage of cultivation;
fifth, the stage of the dharmakāya being non-conditioned.
Sixth, the section on faith;
seventh, the section on comparative evaluation;
eighth, the section on revealing the nature.
Ninth, the section on benefits;
tenth, the section on severing doubts;
eleventh, the section on the non-abiding path.
Twelfth is the section on the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*).
Now, when the Great Sage expounds the Dharma, there must be a specific purpose; thus, there is the introductory section (*nidāna*).

When about to expound the Great Dharma, he necessarily acts for the sake of the bodhisattvas: those who have already attained realization require his empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), while those who have not yet realized it are entrusted to those who have. Therefore, there is the second section on "empowerment and entrustment" (*anuparindanā*).
Since he has already been protected, remembered, and entrusted, and is caused to abide within *prajñā*, there is thus the third section on Abiding.
Although he has attained this abiding, he further advances to cultivate various practices; therefore, next follows the fourth section on Practice.
Because one cultivates the cause of non-attainment, one attains the fruit of the unconditioned; therefore, next is the section clarifying that the Dharma-body is not conditioned.
Since there must be those who believe and accept this teaching of cause and effect, next is the section on the necessity of clarifying the believer.
If one faithfully upholds [this teaching], the merit will be boundless; therefore, there must be a section on "Comparative Evaluation.

The reason why those who uphold and expound it possess boundless merit must stem from the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); if one does not recognize the Buddha-nature, such merit cannot exist. Consequently, there is a section on "Revealing the Nature."
Because the merit cultivated based on the Buddha-nature yields inexhaustible benefits, it is necessary to clarify the Section on Benefits.

In the preceding cycle of teaching, those of sharp faculties have already attained realization, yet those of middling and inferior faculties remain unenlightened and further give rise to doubts; therefore, there is the tenth section, the Section on Severing Doubts.
Once doubt has been eliminated, there is nothing upon which to rely or abide; therefore, there is the eleventh section, the Part on Non-abiding.
This Great Dharma not only benefits the present but also benefits the future; therefore, there is the twelfth section, the Part on Dissemination.
Although these sections are twelve, they do not transcend cause and effect; when their beginning and end are unified, there are generally four cycles.

From the section on "Protective Mindfulness and Entrustment" to the section on "Cultivation," this clarifies the causal dharma-body as being non-conditioned; the section on "The Benefit of the Fruit" then distinguishes the result. This constitutes one cycle clarifying cause and effect.

Next, from the section on "Faith" up to "Comparative Evaluation," this constitutes the cause that brings about the fruit of manifesting the nature; this, then, is the second cycle clarifying cause and effect.

Having clarified the Buddha-nature, the practice based upon that nature constitutes the meaning of the cause; because there is a cause, one attains the fruit, which constitutes the aspect of benefit—this refers to the clarification of cause and effect throughout the three cycles.
Taking the severing of doubt as the cause and non-abiding on the path as the effect thus clarifies the cause and effect from all four sides.

This interpretation has flourished in the northern regions, being transmitted from generation to generation over many years, such that among those who have received instruction, there are none who do not accept and believe it.
I have studied and revered this for many years, yet I have always thought it was not so.
I now ask you: do these twelve divisions originate from the text of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, or are they the commentary of Vasubandhu?
Upon examining the sutras and śāstras now available, none contain such an intention; this is merely the product of human ingenuity fabricating its own interpretations.
The entanglement of the primordial chaos (hundun) is truly detrimental in this regard.
Question:
What fault is there in making this division of the text that you reject it? Answer:
The hindrances are numerous and cannot be recorded in full.
I shall now briefly list several instances to demonstrate where there is obstruction and where there is penetration.
First, by composing this division of the text, one fails to recognize the general and specific aspects of the sūtra.

Why is this so? For instance, as for the introductory section (*nidāna*), it serves as a general introduction to the entire sutra; however, the ten sections such as "protection and entrustment" (*parīndanā*) are specific segments within the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*).
How can one take the general phrasing of a sutra and use it as a precedent for a specific section of the formal exposition? This is a grave error.
Furthermore, you say:
From "the great trichiliocosm of precious treasures" to "giving up a body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," these are termed the section on comparative measurement.
This is merely an error resulting from not understanding the beginning and end of the sutra.

Why is this so? Within this context, the comparative evaluation generally cites two types of giving: external and internal. External giving consists of the three-thousandfold world system and [offerings as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges.
Internal giving likewise comprises two kinds:
First, the practice of directly relinquishing bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
second, the practice of successively offering bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges three times each day.
These represent the ultimate limit of all possible measures of comparison.
Why do you take only the first three types as the standard of comparison, while not taking the "giving up of the body" throughout the three periods of time as a standard of comparison?
This constitutes a fault.

Furthermore, the Treatise states: "From the section on the non-conditioned aspect of the Dharmakāya onwards, all constitute the section for severing doubts. How is it that you alone take the portion from Subhūti’s repeated questioning onwards as the section for severing doubts?

Furthermore, this sutra contains two cycles of exposition, and both the sutras and the treatises make this same distinction; why then do you take the first cycle to constitute many parts and take the second cycle to consolidate them into a single part?
Furthermore, to treat what is great as small is a most serious error.
Moreover, since this section on circulation is indeed a major chapter, it would likewise be improper to treat it according to the precedent of minor sections.
Within this work, the chapters and sentences have been broken down into fragments, even down to the titles of various alternative translations, all of which are corrupt within the sūtras and śāstras;

these textual corruptions shall be fully revealed in due course. Furthermore, some say that since the division into twelve sections is difficult to understand, they have taken the more easily perceived portions and edited them into six chapters.
The six chapters are:
first, the introductory section;
second, the section on protective mindfulness and entrustment.
3. The Section on Abiding;
4. The Section on Practice;
5. The Section on Severing Doubts;
Sixth, the section on circulation.
This kind of discrimination is characteristic of those of inferior learning; their faults remain the same as before, yet their afflictions are even more severe. Why is this so?

If it is argued that the latter section is likewise a portion for severing doubt and thus not further subdivided within the context of severing doubt, then since the former section is also equally not a portion for severing doubt, it too should not have been subdivided within the context of not severing doubt.

Within the section on "Eliminating Doubts" (*vicikitsā-prahāṇa*), there are various meanings; since many parts have already been opened up, for what reason and by what causal conditions is this [specific part] taken as a distinct section?
If that were so, then "wandering for alms while smeared [with ashes]" should also constitute a single section.

If it were the case that the practice of wandering for alms, being part of the introductory section (*nidāna*), was not explained [in detail], then the sections on "Protective Mindfulness" (*ārakṣā*) and "Entrustment" (*parindanā*), which belong to the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*), should likewise not have been explained.
Furthermore, your initial interpretation and subsequent explanation both fail to recognize the general structure of the treatise.

Why is this so? The Master of the Treatise merely explained the difficult passages and omitted the easy phrases; how could later generations, seeing the explanations in the treatise, take them to constitute formal topical divisions (*ko-dan*)?
Furthermore, there is another person who annotates the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* by opening three gates:

from "Thus have I heard" up to "eagerly desires to hear" constitutes the Gate of Causes and Conditions (*nidāna-mukha*), meaning that because these causes and conditions are complete, one is able to expound the *Prajñā*.
From "The Buddha said: 'One should subdue them in this way'" up to "seeing that all marks are non-marks," the gate of the essence of *prajñā* is clarified.
From "He addressed the Buddha: 'Is there any assembly of beings... onwards, the gate of merit is clarified.
However, this explanation does not fully exhaust the meaning.
To which category does the "Circulation" (liú-tōng) belong?
Furthermore, to which category does the subsequent repetition by the Later Zhou belong?
Some say: it is divided into three sections:
first, the introduction;...
Second is the correct exposition;
third is the exposition for circulation.
When the Great Sage expounds the Dharma, it necessarily proceeds by gradual stages; therefore, there is the sequential exposition.
The introductory exposition having been concluded, the main teaching should now be opened; thus there is the "Correct Exposition.
Not only does it provide immediate benefit for the present time, but its influence also extends far into future generations; thus there is the "Exposition on Dissemination."

Now, it is said that interpreting the sūtra according to three explanations poses no contradiction to reason; however, those of the Kaishan school fail to understand the origin and conclusion of these three explanations, and thus they commit an error.
Why is this so? For instance,
taking the questions of Subhūti from the introductory section as a praise and request for the introduction,
while treating the Tathāgata’s response as belonging to the main discourse— this is erroneous.
However, in all sutras, both the questions and the answers are entirely correct; why then do you take the question as the introduction and the answer as the main body?

In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the offerings presented by the assembly at that time serve as the introduction, while Cunda’s request for the teaching and his subsequent inquiries constitute the main body.
In this sutra, the journey to beg for alms serves as the introduction, and Subhūti’s posing of the question should likewise be considered the main body.
The same applies to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: the Tathāgata extensively manifests supernatural transformations as its prologue, and his address to Śāriputra constitutes its main body.
This matter is easy to clarify; one should not treat it with undue confusion.

Furthermore, the threefold exposition is not fixed; although it is presented as an introduction, it does not preclude its being the main teaching, and although it is presented as the main teaching, it does not preclude its being an introduction. The same applies to the dissemination. Why is this so?
Because it introduces the Correct [Section], it is called the "Introduction";
because it corrects the Introduction, it is called the "Correct" [Section].
The Correct Section explains the realization of the Way; having attained this, it is the Correct.
The introduction states that awakening to the Way is likewise attained through this correctness.
Now, for the sake of a general explanation, I have opened up three different [approaches].
Within these three, each is further divided into two sections.
There are two kinds of prefaces:
first, the general preface;
second, the specific preface.
The main body consists of two parts:
first, the extensive explanation;
second, the concise explanation.
The dissemination [of the sūtra] has two parts:
first, concluding the Buddha’s discourse on the sūtra;
second, clarifying that the assembly rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
Within the two sections of the introduction, there are four pairs:
first, the general;
second, the specific.
"Universal" (tong) takes "sameness" as its meaning; since the six matters in all sūtras are identical, it is called the universal introduction (tongxu).

"Particular" (bie) takes "difference" as its meaning; since these vary from sūtra to sūtra—whether it be parents sending a letter, an elder offering a parasol, the heavens raining four kinds of flowers, or [the Buddha] begging for food while smeared with mud—it is called the particular introduction (biexu).

Next, regarding the "Sequence for Witnessing Faith" (samyak-pratyaya-nidāna) and the "Sequence of the Arousing" (nidāna): these six matters are established so as to inspire faith in people; therefore, it is called the Sequence for Witnessing Faith.
Walking for alms to initiate the True Sūtra is called the Sequence of the Arousing.

Next, the "Preface to the Bequeathed Teachings" and the "Preface to the Present Occasion" clarify that as the Tathāgata was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, Ānanda’s mind sank into an ocean of grief, such that he could not compose himself.
Aniruddha said: "You are one who upholds the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha; whatever you wish to ask, you must ask while there is still time.
Thereupon, Ānanda posed four questions, the last of which was:
"What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?
The Buddha said:
"At the beginning of all sūtras, one should establish the phrase: 'Thus have I heard.'"
Because this testament instructs that these six matters be maintained, it is called the "Preface to the Bequeathed Teaching" (Yijiao xu).
Since the events such as begging for alms occurred at the very time the sutra was being preached, they are called the "Prologue of the Present Occasion" (Xianqian xu).
Next are the preface and the postscript to the sutra.
These six matters, which occur after the preaching of the sutra has concluded, are called the postscript.
Those matters concerning the practice of begging for alms that occur prior to the preaching of the sutra are called the preface.
Question: For what reasons and conditions did the Buddha require that these six matters be placed at the beginning of all sutras? Answer:
For the sake of establishing faith and confidence, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By specifying the time, place, and person, one causes people to give rise to faith.

Furthermore, all non-Buddhist teachers habitually place auspicious formulas at the beginning of their scriptures; as the *Śata-śāstra* says: "The masters who composed their treatises were selective, yet all of them spoke of auspiciousness at the outset."
Now, because one wishes to distinguish [this teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), it is structured according to six points.
A question is asked:

"If these six points are established in order to distinguish them from the non-Buddhists, yet the non-Buddhists also claim to establish these same six points, how does this distinguish [your teaching]?"
Answer: This clarifies that these are the six matters of *prajñā*; therefore, they are used to establish faith and distinguish [the Buddhist path] from that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Regarding faith in *prajñā*, this is a faith that is without reliance and without attainment; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Not believing in any phenomena is called believing in *prajñā*."
Because all dharmas are non-arising, it is called the arising of prajñā;
because one does not believe in any dharmas, it is called having faith in prajñā.
Tenth, the correct explanation of the text.
"Thus have I heard. Regarding the six matters of the general introduction, "thus" (evam) refers to:
first, clarifying the Dharma that was heard.
Question: The Buddha is the Omniscient One; he attained awakening by himself without a teacher and did not learn from others. Why, then, does he say, "Thus have I heard"?
If he says, "Thus have I heard," it implies he heard it from another, and thus he would not be omniscient.
Answer: This has already been explained previously; this is not the Buddha himself declaring, "Thus have I heard," but rather an instruction to his attendant to say, "I have heard.
Furthermore, this refers to the great disciples such as Ānanda declaring, "Thus have I heard," as stated in the *Dharmaskandha* (The Collection of the Dharma):
Ānanda ascended the high seat, and Mahākāśyapa asked him,
"In what place did you first preach the Dharma?
Ānanda joined his palms toward the direction of Nirvāṇa and replied to Mahākāśyapa:
"Thus have I heard: when the Buddha was first at the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma for the five bhikṣus.
For this reason, it is not the Buddha himself who makes this claim.

Paramārtha Tripiṭaka Master, citing Vasubandhu’s commentary, states: "When Ānanda was about to recite the Dharma-piṭaka, he ascended the seat of fearlessness and transformed his body to resemble that of the Buddha, possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs."
At that time, the great assembly gave rise to three kinds of doubt:
first, they wondered whether Śākyamuni, though having previously entered extinction, had now appeared once more to preach the Dharma for them;
second, they wondered whether Śākyamuni had already passed away and this was another Buddha from another direction who had come.
Third, it is said that although Śākyamuni has passed away, Ānanda, being a disciple of the Buddha, has now attained Buddhahood and acts as his successor.
Because of these three doubts, Ānanda immediately dispelled them by stating, "Thus have I heard.
This clarifies that while the Tathāgata has thus passed away, he heard [the teachings] from the Buddha's presence; it does not refer to the three aforementioned matters.
Regarding the phrase "Thus" (*evam*), more than twenty masters have offered interpretations; I shall now briefly mention them without further elaboration.
First, according to the explanation of Nāgārjuna: "Thus" means that in the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is that by which one enters, and wisdom is that by which one crosses over.
That which is thus is precisely faith.
Because of faith, one says, "This matter is thus"; if one lacks faith, one says, "This matter is not thus.
Now, it is through faith that one gains entry into the Buddha-dharma; for this reason, the sūtra begins by stating, "Thus have I heard."

Regarding faith in prajñā: it clarifies that prajñā is without dependence, without attainment, and without conceptual proliferation; because it is ultimately pure and truly trustworthy, one enters into prajñā by means of this faith.
Next, Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "In this way" refers to the sense of certainty.
Briefly, two types are clarified:
first, the teaching in this way; [second, the realization in this way].
"Second, the principle is such as the teaching.
Regarding "such as this" (evam), there are generally several meanings:
first, because it accords with the measure of the Buddha's teachings, it is called "such as this."
Why is this so? The Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught the Dharma extensively, taught it with moderate detail, or taught it concisely.
Now, as Ānanda transmits the True Dharma, he does so according to the Buddha’s own extensive or concise teachings, neither adding nor subtracting anything; therefore, he says, "Thus."
Second, these Buddhas teach in this sequential manner.
Why is this? All teachings of the Dharma generally consist of six matters:
First, the initiation;
second, the brief presentation of the thesis;
third, the detailed explanation.
Fourth, the refutation;
fifth, the resolution;
sixth, the entrustment for circulation to Ānanda.
Now, in order to recite and uphold the Buddha’s words in their proper sequence, it is said:
"Thus" (evam). Thirdly, because it accords with the title of the sutra, it is said: "Thus.
To transmit and maintain the Buddha's scriptures, one must know the name of the sutra.
If one does not know the title of a sutra, how can one understand its meaning? Why is this so?

Because the title of a sutra encompasses the entirety of that sutra; for example, although the chapters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Sūtra number ninety, they are collectively titled the *Mahāprajñā*. Thus, by means of the name "Mahā," the meaning of all ninety chapters is subsumed.
For this reason, one must know the name of the sutra.
Because Ānanda recited and upheld it according to its name, he said, "Thus.
Fourth, regarding the causal conditions being "thus": the causal conditions for the Buddhas of the three periods of time in preaching the sutras briefly comprise four meanings:
First, one must possess fundamental omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) before being able to preach the sutras;
second, one must possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) before preaching the Dharma;
third, one must do so in order to repay the debt of gratitude for the True Dharma (*saddharma*) before preaching the Dharma.
Fourth is decisive realization through faith, which has four aspects:

first, knowing that there is a specific time for preaching the sūtra; second, knowing the location where the sūtra is preached; third, knowing that the one who preaches is indeed the Tathāgata; and fourth, knowing that there is an assembly of listeners.
Regarding the time, place, audience, and speaker, what I have spoken is truly worthy of faith and acceptance; therefore, it is called "thus" (*evam*).
As for the principle being "thus": to say that the principle exists is termed the view of existence (*astitva-dṛṣṭi*);
to say that the principle does not exist is termed the wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
To say "both existent and non-existent" is called the view of contradiction;
to say "neither existent nor non-existent" is called the view of delusion.
If the principle being elucidated falls into any of these four positions, it cannot be called suchness.
Now, being free from these four types of denial and having nothing upon which to rely, it is called "thus.
Regarding the phrase "I have heard," this second part clarifies the person who hears.
Regarding the term "I," the reason Ānanda refers to himself as "I" is, first, because he wishes to testify that he heard this directly from the Buddha's presence and not by hearsay. Why is this so?
First, because I have now heard this directly from the Tathāgata, I am thus addressed as "I.
Second, because it is intended to manifest that Ānanda’s vows and practices in past lives have been fulfilled, I am thus addressed as "I."

Ānanda has cultivated extensive learning for immeasurable kalpas; by the power of his original vows, he has attained dhāraṇī, such that once it passes through his ears, it is never lost, nor does he need to ask again—just as when water is poured from one vessel into another.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "I and Ānanda simultaneously resolved to attain enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja; yet because I delighted in diligent effort, I have consequently attained Buddhahood."
Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning; therefore, he upholds my Dharma-treasury. Furthermore, as a sutra says:

"In the past, Śākyamuni was a śrāmaṇera under Kāśyapa Buddha. His teacher limited himself to reciting a thousand words of scripture each day while also going out to beg for food on his behalf. Fearing that he would not be able to complete his recitation, the śrāmaṇera was filled with one-pointed anxiety."

At that time, Ānanda was acting as the elder. Seeing the śrāmaṇera’s sorrowful expression on the road, he asked him the reason for it, whereupon the śrāmaṇera related the aforementioned matters in detail.
The elder then said to the śrāmaṇera:
"I shall provide you with food every day so that you may recite the sūtras with a peaceful mind; do not be distressed anymore."
The elder made a vow, saying:
"If this śrāmaṇera attains Buddhahood, I shall become his foremost disciple for the sake of the Dharma-treasury.
Because this demonstrates the fulfillment of his past vow, he is called "I."
Third, because of his sovereignty, he is called "I. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Ānanda is fully endowed with extensive learning and wisdom;
yet all sentient beings cannot simultaneously grasp and comprehend the Buddha's words."
Even if one were able to fully comprehend them, without the power of dhāraṇī, one could not recollect them without forgetting;
and even if one possessed such recollection without forgetting, one would still be unable to fully possess the three types of wisdom.
"One who lacks mastery over hearing the Dharma cannot be called 'self.
'Self' carries the meaning of mastery.
Now Ānanda is able to fully comprehend the Buddha’s words all at once, and is also able to retain them forever without forgetting."
Fourth, because they are fully endowed with the generation of the three types of wisdom and have attained mastery within the hearing of the Dharma, they are called "I.
Question: The Buddha-dharma is selfless; for what reason are they called "I"?

Answer: The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Within the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self; yet, in order to guide sentient beings, one speaks of 'self' as a provisional designation."
Therefore, there is no fault.
As for the term "heard" (*śruta*), it is so called because it possesses several meanings:
first, to manifest the virtue of the person from whom one has heard.

What Ānanda has heard was not heard from non-Buddhists, nor from the disciples of the Buddha, nor from sages, nor from emanated beings, nor from the various devas; what he has now heard was heard from the One Possessed of All-Knowledge.
Second, it is to manifest that the Dharma one has heard is most supreme.
It clarifies that the names, phrases, and syllables of the Buddha-dharma are skillful and elegant, while its principles and meanings are profound and pure.
As for the teachings of non-Buddhists, they possess only mere words but lack any true meaning.
If one hears the Buddha-dharma, it is called "correct hearing.
Third, the principle revealed is most supreme.
The Buddha-dharma and the true path are perfectly complete and without inversion; because they are taught in accordance with reality, it is called "correct teaching."
To hear in accordance with reality is called "right hearing.
Fourth, because it is the most excellent practice, it is called "right hearing.
To practice in reliance upon the true teaching is the most excellent among all practices; therefore, it is called "right hearing."
Fifth, because one attains the correct fruit through practice, it is called "correct hearing.
The correct fruit is what is known as Great Parinirvāṇa.
Question:
Is it by means of the deity that one hears?
Is it by means of consciousness that one hears?
Or is it by means of the sense organ that one hears?
Is it through the conjunction [of the faculties] that one hears? If it were the self (*ātman*) that hears, why does the self employ the ear to hear and not the eye?
If it were consciousness (*vijñāna*) that hears, the same objection applies.
If the sense organ were to hear by itself, there would be no time when consciousness is present, and thus the empty organ should be able to hear;
if each [factor] individually cannot hear, then even in combination they still cannot hear.
Based on this principle, there is ultimately no such thing as hearing.
The answer is:
what is now called "hearing" is hearing by way of causes and conditions.
To hear through causes and conditions is to hear what is not heard; it is to hear while there is nothing heard.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The one who preaches the Dharma has no preaching and no demonstration;
the one who listens to the Dharma has no hearing and no attainment."
"The Tathāgata has said nothing, and Ānanda has heard nothing; it is through such speaking and hearing that they can be mutually established.
As for "at one time," this is the third [point], clarifying the time when the teaching was spoken.
Just as when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, it is a time when those precious objects can be obtained;
and just as when a Tathāgata appears in the world, it is a time when the Dharma-treasure can be obtained—therefore, it is called "at one time."
Second, it is called "at one time" because when all sentient beings who are crazed or deaf hear what the Tathāgata speaks, they attain awakening; thus it is called "one time.
Furthermore, there is the time of the true teacher, the time of the true teaching, and the time of true study; therefore, it is called "one time."
When these three conditions are present, sentient beings attain the Way.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Because the True Dharma, the teacher, and the listener are difficult to encounter."
If one possesses these three kinds [of conditions], then birth and death have an end;
if one does not possess these three kinds, then birth and death are endless.
Furthermore, as long as sentient beings have not yet planted the seed of faith, it cannot be called "one time."
Now, when the Prajñā is being taught, it is the time for planting the seeds of inferior faith;
once the seeds of faith have been planted, it is the time for the growth of right contemplation;
and once right contemplation has grown, it is the time for the perfection of the roots of goodness; therefore, it is said to be "at one time."
Furthermore, because Ānanda was able to fully comprehend the Buddha’s teaching all at once, it is called "at one time.
Moreover, because it was adapted to the faculties and conditions of those present at that particular moment, it is called "at one time."

Why is this so? The teachings of the Buddhas differ in their breadth and brevity; that the Prajñāpāramitā is now taught in brief is simply because it accords with the specific faculties and conditions of those present at this time.
Furthermore, one must understand that this *prajñā* is "at once.
Regarding "at once": "time" is a provisional term for what is not time; "one" is a provisional term for what is not one.
"Buddha" refers to the fourth heading, the master who proclaims the teaching.
Although the three matters have been set forth above, right and wrong have not yet been distinguished;
only by designating the Buddha in the fourth [section] are gain and loss clearly revealed. Why is this so?
Although it is said, "Thus have I heard at one time," it was not yet known from whom this was heard; therefore, it is now stated that it was heard from the Buddha and not from anyone else.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"Bhagavān" means that he is able to sever the afflictions and possesses great merit; thus, he is named Bhagavān.
Regarding "abiding," there are two kinds:
first, external abiding;
second, internal abiding.
Regarding what is called "dwelling outside," there are generally four types:
first, dwelling in a place of royal transformation, which refers to Śākyamuni’s residence in Sahā;
second, dwelling apart from the secular world, which refers to residing within all monasteries (saṃghārāma).
Third, abiding in deportment (*airyāpathika*), which refers to walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all being termed "abiding";
fourth, abiding by not having relinquished the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which refers to the Tathāgata’s not yet having entered parinirvāṇa.
There are four types of internal abiding:
first, the celestial abiding, which consists of abiding in generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth;
second, the Brahma abiding, which consists of abiding in the four immeasurable minds.
Third is the noble dwelling, which dwells in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
fourth is the Buddha-dwelling, which dwells within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This is the non-dwelling and non-non-dwelling of *prajñā*; for the sake of sentient beings, it is conventionally designated as "dwelling."
Regarding "Śrāvastī," this is the fifth [section], clarifying the place of residence.
There are two kinds of places:
first, general places; [second, specific places].
Second is the specific location.
Śrāvastī is the general location, while the Jeta Grove Monastery is the specific location.
Question:

For what reason does the Buddha dwell frequently in Rājagṛha and Śrāvastī? Answer: Because the Buddha previously accepted the invitation of King Bimbisāra, he dwells in Rājagṛha; because he previously accepted the invitation of King Prasenajit, he dwells in Śrāvastī. Furthermore, the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha because it is the capital of Magadha, a land of great power and vast territory, where the people are numerous and the offerings are abundant. He dwells in Śrāvastī because it is the capital of Kosala, a land of great power and vast territory, where the people are numerous and the offerings are abundant. Moreover, the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha because it is the place where the Tathāgata attained supreme enlightenment and turned the wheel of the Dharma; he dwells in Śrāvastī because it is the place where he performed various great miraculous displays and defeated the heretics. Furthermore, the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha because it is the place where he subdued the dragon Āśvatarī and converted the elder Ghoṣila; he dwells in Śrāvastī because it is the place where he subdued the dragon Apalāla and converted the elder Sudatta. Furthermore, the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha because it is the place where he received the offering of the seven treasures from King Bimbisāra; he dwells in Śrāvastī because it is the place where he received the offering of the Jetavana Grove from the elder Sudatta. Furthermore, the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha because it is the place where he received the offering of the Bamboo Garden from King Bimbisāra; he dwells in Śrāvastī because it is the place where he received the offering of the Eastern Park from the courtesan Āmrapālī. Furthermore, the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha because it is the place where he received the offering of the Vulture Peak from King Bimbisāra; he dwells in Śrāvastī because it is the place where he received the offering of the Saptaparṇa Cave from the elder Sudatta. Furthermore, the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha because it is the place where he received the offering of the Gabled Hall from King Bimbisāra; he dwells in Śrāvastī because it is the place where he received the offering of the Perfumed Chamber from the elder Sudatta. Next, because he accepted the invitation of Sudatta, he resided in Śrāvastī.
Furthermore, because he wished to repay the kindness of the Dharma-body, he resided in Rājagṛha;
and because he wished to repay the kindness of the birth-body, he resided in Śrāvastī.
Why is this so? Because the Buddha attained the Way in Rājagṛha, in the kingdom of Magadha; therefore, in order to repay the kindness of the Dharma-body, he dwells in Rājagṛha.
Question:

The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu in Central India; the present city of Śrāvastī is a country in Eastern India. Why, then, is it said that he resided in the city of Śrāvastī for the sake of repaying the kindness of his birth-body?
Answer:
The Buddha’s ancestral origin was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī in Eastern India; it was only later that he came to the city of Kapilavastu in Central India.
Since his name is established based on his origin, it is said that he dwelt in the kingdom of Śrāvastī out of gratitude for the kindness of his birthplace.
Furthermore, because there were many people and things in Rājagṛha and the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the Buddha wished to teach and transform sentient beings in places where there were many people.

As stated in the sūtras, there were nine hundred million households in the kingdom of Śrāvastī; as told in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, there were one billion eight hundred million people.
Furthermore, because these two countries produce many people of great wisdom as well as the likes of the six heretical teachers, the Buddha dwells frequently in this city.
Question:
For what reason is it named Śrāvastī?
Answer: A master from the northern regions says:
In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, there were two brothers who were rishis; the younger brother was named Śepha, which means "the young one."
The elder brother was called Ābhāpṛthivī, which means "Unassailable" (Abhaya).
These two brothers dwelt in this place seeking the Way, and it was named after them.
The younger brother omitted "bhā," while the elder brother omitted "ā"; taking both names together, it is thus called Śrāvastī.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said: "The correct pronunciation of that country should be *Śrāvastī*, which in this [Chinese] language means 'Country of Good Renown.
In the past, there was a rishi who possessed great renown and resided therein; it was named after this rishi, hence it is called the 'Country of Good Renown.'"
It is further said: "This land possesses four meanings:
first, it is replete with many jewels;
second, the people therein largely enjoy the pleasures of the five senses."
Third, there are the virtues of the dharmas; in this land, people practice giving and precepts extensively, which are called "dharma-virtues.

Fourth, regarding the future attainment of the fruit of liberation: this clarifies that the people of this land will, in the future, mostly be reborn among humans and devas and attain the fruit of liberation.
Because these four qualities were heard of far away in other lands, it is called the Land of Good Renown (*Khyen-ming*).

Previously, it was translated as the Land of Renowned Goods (*Mun-wu*); because many fine goods are produced in this land and their fame spreads to all countries from afar, it is named the Land of Renowned Goods.
The *Dvādaśayojana-sūtra* states: "There is no place that does not exist, yet this [place] excels all others.
Question:
For how many years did the Buddha reside in Śrāvastī?

Answer: The Sūtra says: "While residing in the kingdom of Śrāvastī for twenty-five years, there were nine hundred million households. Three hundred million households saw the Buddha but did not hear the Dharma; three hundred million households both heard the Dharma and saw the Buddha; and three hundred million households neither saw the Buddha nor heard the Dharma."
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated: "He resided in Śrāvastī for seven years from beginning to end, and resided in Rājagṛha for four years.
This remains undetermined at present.
Question:
Where did the King’s City (Rājagṛha) and Śrāvastī previously reside?
Answer: It is said:
The Buddha was previously residing in Rājagṛha and later moved to Śrāvastī.
The phrase "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park" refers to the second [section], which is designated as a specific location.
Question:
For what causes and conditions was this Jeta Grove Monastery established? Answer:
This is explained in detail in such sūtras as the *Dvādaśayanīya-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.

As stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*: "The King of Śrāvastī, Prasenajit, had a great minister named Sudatta. This man lived at home with immense wealth and boundless treasures; he delighted in practicing charity, providing relief to the poor and destitute, as well as to the orphaned and the elderly."
The people of that time consequently gave him the title Anāthapiṇḍada, meaning "Giver of Alms to the Destitute.
At that time, the elder fathered seven sons; when they had all grown up, he arranged for them to be married, continuing in order until the sixth.

He had a seventh son who was exceptionally handsome and extraordinary; he cherished him with particular affection and intended to marry him off. He sought for his son a girl of exquisite beauty, perfect countenance, and auspicious marks.
He then spoke to the brahmins, saying, "Who has a daughter of excellent appearance and endowed with all the auspicious marks? You should seek her out for me.

The brahmins then began their search, traveling from place to place until they reached the city of Rājagṛha. There was a high minister there named Ratnapāla, whose wealth was immeasurable and who had faith and reverence for the Triple Gem.

At that time, a brahmin arrived at his house to beg for alms. According to the custom of that country, when giving things to others, a young girl was required to hold the object while making the offering.
At that time, the elder Ratnarakṣita had a daughter whose appearance was upright and whose complexion was exceptionally beautiful; she came out holding food to offer it to the brahmin.
When the brahmin saw this, his heart was filled with great joy, thinking,
"The one I have been seeking is surely this very person!
He then asked the girl:
"Has anyone come to seek you out?
The girl replied,
"No one has yet."
He asked again: "Young woman!
Is your father at home?"
The woman replied, "It is here. The brāhmaṇa said:
"Please let him come outside; I wish to see him and converse with him.
Then the daughter went inside and said to her father, "A guest has arrived outside and wishes to see you."
The father then came out.
At that time, the brahmin inquired after his health and well-being, asking whether he was at ease and free from ailment.
Once the greetings were concluded, he spoke to the elder, saying:
"In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a high minister named Sudatta, who served as the state counselor.
Do you know him? He replied:
"I have not seen that person, but I have heard of his name.
He replied, "Do you know him?"
"That man is the foremost in wealth and status in that city of Śrāvastī, and you are likewise the most eminent in wealth and status here.
Suḍatta has a son who is handsome, extraordinary, and full of remarkable qualities; he wishes to take your daughter as his wife—is this acceptable to you?"
He replied, "So be it!

At that time, before the Brahmin had yet returned home, he encountered some merchants coming to Śrāvastī; he immediately used them to send a letter back to Sudatta, reporting the matter in full detail.
Upon receiving the letter, Sudatta was filled with joy and immediately went to King Prasenajit to request a brief period of leave in order to arrange a marriage for his son.
The king granted his request at once.
Thereupon, carrying a great load of precious treasures, he set out for Rājagṛha. Along the way, he relieved the poor and destitute.
Upon reaching Rājagṛha, he went to the house of Ratnākara to seek a wife for his son from Ratnākara.
The elder welcomed him with joy and provided bedding and seating; he stayed the night in his house, where the interior was bustling as food and drink were prepared.
Sudatta thought to himself:
"What sacrificial offerings has this householder prepared?
What does he intend to do?
Is it not that he wishes to invite the king, the crown prince, high ministers, or perhaps those related by marriage?"
He then asked him, saying:
"Householder, why is it that this evening you have personally undertaken such tasks and prepared these offerings? Is it because you wish to invite the king, the crown prince, or the ministers?"
He replied, "No. He asked again:
"Are you intending to arrange a marriage or hold a gathering for relatives? He replied, "No!"
He asked again, "What will you do? He replied:
"I wish to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus tomorrow.
At that time, when Sudatta heard the names of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, his hair stood on end with solemn reverence, and his heart and mind were filled with joy according to what he had attained.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
I pray that you will explain its meaning."
The elder replied: "Have you not heard?
The son of King Śuddhodana, named Siddhārtha, on the day of his birth, was attended by celestial deities who manifested auspicious omens; he immediately took seven steps and proclaimed:"
"Throughout heaven and on earth, I alone am the most honored!
Hearing such auspicious words, Sudatta was filled with joy and exultation; moved by deep faith and reverence, he desired to see the Buddha this very night.
Thereupon, the heavens became bright, and he departed. At midnight, he went out and saw a celestial shrine;
he immediately paid his respects, but suddenly forgot his mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. As dawn approached and it grew dark again, he thought to himself: "It is dark tonight;
if I go now, I will surely be harmed by evil spirits or fierce beasts. I shall return to the city for now and wait until dawn before departing."
At that moment, a deity in the sky, seeing his desire to repent, descended and spoke:
"Householder, do not regret!
I am your former spiritual friend, the brahmin Madhu-skandha; because I heard the Dharma, I was reborn among the devas."
Go and see the Buddha; you will obtain immeasurable benefit.

Even if you were to obtain a hundred wagons of precious jewels today, or even if the four continents of this world-system were filled with such treasures, it would not equal the benefit obtained by lifting your feet and proceeding to the presence of the World-Honored One—a benefit that exceeds those by a hundred thousandfold.
"Go now; do not regret it!
Having heard these words spoken by the deva, Sudatta’s sense of reverence increased all the more.
Thereupon, having emerged from darkness back into clear light, he immediately followed the path and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Knowing that Sudatta was approaching at that time, the Buddha went outside to practice walking meditation.

Then, from afar, Sudatta saw the World-Honored One, who resembled a mountain of gold; his marks and signs and majestic countenance were solemn and brilliantly manifest. Upon seeing him, his heart rejoiced, yet not knowing the proper etiquette for greeting, he asked the World-Honored One directly:
"I wonder, Gautama, how you are faring?"
The World-Honored One immediately bade them take their seats.

At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven saw from afar that although Sudatta had beheld the World-Honored One, he did not know how to prostrate at his feet. The gods then manifested as four men in a procession and approached the place where the World-Honored One was. They grasped the Buddha’s feet and paid homage, knelt for a long time to inquire after his well-being, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Sudatta, seeing this, was struck with amazement and thought to himself:
"The ritual of reverence ought indeed to be such as this."
He immediately rose from his seat, paid his respects, inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him:
the subtle and wondrous Four Noble Truths—suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
Having heard the Dharma with joy, he immediately realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Thereupon, he addressed the Buddha:
"I pray only that the Tathāgata will bestow his compassion upon the sentient beings within the great city of Śrāvastī, leading them away from the heterodox and toward the orthodox!"
The World-Honored One replied:
"The way of those who have left the household life differs from that of the laity; their places of residence ought to be distinct.
Since they have no vihāra there, how can they go?"
At that time, Sudatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Your disciple is able to rise; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
The World-Honored One remained silent.
Sudatta took his leave and departed, whereupon he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Upon my return to my native land, I shall construct a vihāra."
‘We do not know the method for polishing; we only pray that the World-Honored One will send a disciple with us to instruct and demonstrate it.
The World-Honored One reflected:
‘Within the city of Śrāvastī, the brahmins believe in heterodox and inverted views; if any other person were to go, they certainly would not be able to accomplish this.’
"Only Śāriputra is of Brahmin lineage; he has been intelligent since his youth and is endowed with supernatural powers. His departure will surely be beneficial.
He was then immediately summoned to go together with Sudatta.
Thereupon, they returned to Śrāvastī and traveled together with Śāriputra to inspect various sites to find a location that was level and spacious enough to construct a vihāra.

They searched everywhere, yet found no place that met their requirements; however, Prince Jeta alone possessed a garden whose ground was level and even, whose trees were lush and flourishing, and which was neither too near nor too far—truly the perfect site.
Then Śāriputra said to Sudatta:
"This garden site is suitable for the construction of a vihāra.
If it were built at a great distance, alms would be difficult to obtain."
"If it were close by, it would be noisy and distracting, hindering and obstructing the practice of the Path. Sudatta was delighted;
he went to the Prince's residence and said to him, "I now wish to erect a vihāra for the Tathāgata. Only the Prince’s garden is suitable for this purpose; I wish to purchase it."
The Prince smiled and said, "What am I lacking?
This garden is lush and flourishing; it is intended for my recreation. Why do you wish to purchase it?"

Sudatta was thus persistent and would not desist. The Prince then jokingly replied, "If you can cover the ground with gold such that there is no empty space between the pieces, then I shall grant it to you."
Sudatta then respectfully agreed, loaded gold, and spread it over the ground according to the price.
The Prince said, "I was just speaking in jest; how can you buy it so readily?"
Sudatta replied, "According to the law for a crown prince, one should not speak in jest;
to utter such falsehoods is not to say that the heir apparent is incapable of succeeding to the throne."
He immediately went with the Prince to the place where the judges presided.

At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, intending to build a vihāra for the Buddha, feared that the judges and ministers would be partial toward the Prince; he therefore manifested as a man acting as a judge and said to the Prince:
"Now, a prince should not speak falsely or engage in idle jesting."
"Since you have already agreed to sell, it is not fitting to regret it midway.
He then finalized the sale of the park to Sudatta.

Sudatta was overjoyed and immediately dispatched men with elephants and horses to carry gold, spreading it across eighty *qǐng*. In a mere moment, it was nearly complete, with only a small portion of land remaining.
Sudatta reflected:
"From which treasury shall I draw forth enough gold?
It must be neither too much nor too little to be exactly sufficient."
Jeta asked, "Do you dislike the height? You wish to buy the terrace. He replied:
He thought to himself, "I must surely find some store of gold sufficient to satisfy him;
I shall fill it for him. Jeta thought to himself, "The Buddha must possess great virtue, for he has caused this man to treat his wealth so lightly."
He then said: "Stop at this point!
Do not offer any more gold."
"The garden belongs to you, but the trees belong to me; I shall personally build a gate-tower for the Buddha.
Sudatta was delighted and immediately returned home to begin the construction work.
When the six teachers heard this, they immediately went to inform the king:

"The elder Sudatta has purchased the prince’s garden, intending to build a vihāra for Gautama. We request permission to compete with him in the display of spiritual arts; if we prevail, then let him be allowed to proceed with its construction."
The King immediately summoned the elder and questioned him:
"Now the six teachers say:
'Have you purchased Prince Jeta’s grove to erect a vihāra for Gautama?'"

He sought to compete his spiritual arts with a disciple of the Śramaṇa; if he were to emerge victorious, he might then proceed with the construction, but if he could not, he would not be permitted to build.
The elder returned home, put on soiled and greasy clothes, and was distressed and unhappy.
The next day, Śāriputra donned his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the elder’s house; seeing that he was unhappy, he immediately asked, "For what reason is this?"
The elder replied, "I fear that the construction of the vihāra will not be completed; for this reason, I am grieved. Śāriputra said:

"For what reason? He replied, "Now the six heretical teachers have come to the King to challenge him to a contest of spiritual arts; only when the Venerable One has emerged victorious shall they be permitted to rise."
"If he is not their equal, then we shall not permit it.

However, these six teachers have been ordained for a long time; they have long studied various arts and skills such that none can surpass them. We do not yet know whether you, Venerable One, are able to compete with them in the display of spiritual powers."
Śāriputra replied:
"Even if the followers of the Six Heretics were to fill the trichiliocosm, as numerous as a grove of bamboo, they could not move a single hair of mine."
"If you wish to compete in arts, simply allow them to do as they please.
The elder was delighted; he changed into new clothes and went to inform the king, saying, "The six teachers wish to compete; let them follow their own will."
The King immediately informed the six teachers and proclaimed to the people of the kingdom:
"Seven days hence, outside the city walls, the six teachers shall compete with the śramaṇa in the display of their spiritual arts."
"In that kingdom there were eighteen billion people.
At that time, according to the laws of that country, the multitude was assembled by striking drums: if the bronze drum was struck, twelve billion people would assemble;
if the silver drum was beaten, fourteen billion people would assemble."
If the golden drum were sounded, everyone would assemble.
When the seven days had elapsed, the drum was struck and everyone gathered; the assembly of the six masters numbered three hundred million people.
At that time, the people all prepared seats for the King and the six teachers.

Then, the elder prepared a seat for Śāriputra; however, at that moment, Śāriputra was beneath a tree, having entered a state of tranquil meditative concentration (*samādhi*), traversing various dhyāna-gates with unimpeded mastery. He thought to himself:
"The great assembly in this gathering has practiced heterodox ways for a long time, and they are arrogant and self-exalting."
"What virtue should I employ to subdue these sentient beings?
Having reflected thus, he immediately made this vow:
"If, throughout countless kalpas, I have practiced loving-kindness and filial piety toward my parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, then as I now enter the assembly, let all people pay homage to me."
At that time, the assembly of the six teachers had already gathered, yet Śāriputra alone had not yet arrived. They then addressed the king, saying:
"The disciple of Gautama knows himself to be without skill; he has not come out of fear."
The King asked the elder,
"Where is your teacher now?
Sudatta immediately went to where Śāriputra was and said:
"The great assembly has gathered; I pray that you will come to this meeting.
At that time, Śāriputra arose from his meditative concentration and, having adjusted his robes with composure, proceeded toward the assembly like a lion king.
At that time, the great assembly and the six heretical teachers, beholding his appearance, suddenly rose up like grass bent by the wind, unconsciously performing a prostration.
Then Śāriputra ascended the seat spread out by Sudatta.
